# Review — aeneid-043 (Aeneid VI.295–397), adversarial reviewer

Two passes. In pass 1, I checked each of the 49 units word by word: `l`, `i` and `n` against the Latin, every grammatical label, the speech marks, the factual and memory claims, and every `i` for remembered English. The flagged lines got the closest check: 305–312, 326, 362, 365, 371 and 376. Pass 2 re-read every edited unit.

I then hand-scanned all 103 lines by quantities and compared each with the scanner's output. The scanner was run in-process exactly as `build_aeneid.py` runs `SL.scan_story`. Each new `scan-fixes.json` entry was checked against a replica of the build's word-match rule and of the validator's six-foot rule. With the fixes applied, all 103 lines pass.

`t` is untouched. The cut tuples in `make_units.py` are unchanged (checked by script), and the regenerated `units.json` has identical `t`, `ln` and `p` in all 49 units. `title`, `titleEn`, `part` and `about` are unchanged. `units.json` was regenerated by `make_units.py`; `build_aeneid.py` was not run.

Speech marks: `t` has 6 “ and 6 ”, `l` has 7/7 and `i` has 6/6. The extra pair in `l` is “Tell me,” he says, “O maiden at 318. Speeches open at 318, 322, 341, 347, 373 and 388 and close at 320, 330, 346, 371, 381 and 397.

**Severity counts: major 5, medium 6, low 37. Refused findings: 12 (listed at the end). Misprints: none.**

## Changes

### Major
1. **6.307 scan wrong** (unflagged, cost 0). The scanner gave a valid-looking hexameter with the wrong quantities. It made *magnănimum* -na- long and *hērōum* he-, -ro- short. Hand scansion: māg-nă-nĭ | (mum) hē-rō | ūm pŭ-ĕ | (ri) in-nūp | tae-quĕ pŭ | el-lae.
2. **6.322 scan wrong** (unflagged). The scanner read *Anchīsā* with -chi- and -sa short and *gĕnĕrāte* with ge- and ne- long. Hand scansion: An-chī | sā gĕ-nĕ | rā-tĕ dĕ | um cer | tis-sĭ-mă | prō-les. This matches *Anchisa satus* at 331, which the scanner gets right.
3. **6.337 scan wrong** (unflagged). The scanner made *sēsē* short-short and gave *Pălĭnūrus* long Pa- and li-. Hand scansion: Ec-cĕ gŭ | bēr-nā | tōr sē | sē Pă-lĭ | nū-rŭs ă | gē-bat.
4. **6.378 scan wrong** (unflagged). The scanner made *fīnĭtĭmī* all long and the adverbs *longē* and *lātē* short. Hand scansion: Nam tŭ-ă | fī-nĭ-tĭ | mī lon | gē lā | tē-quĕ pĕr | ur-bēs.
5. **Note 322–324, `di cuius iurare timent et fallere numen`**: the note gave "'Di cuius… timent' is 'whose divinity the gods fear'". That makes `numen` the object of `timent`, which is a misparse. `Timent` takes the two infinitives, and `cuius… numen` is their object. The note now says so. `l` was rebuilt to match ("whose divinity the gods fear to swear by and to play false").

### Medium
6–8. **Scan, the known blind spots**:
   - **6.317**: *Aeneas* was split into A-e-ne. The fix is Ae-nē | ās mī | rā-tŭs ĕ | nim mō | tus-quĕ tŭ | mul-tū.
   - **6.364** (packet flag, COSTLY 2.0): the scanner read *Iuli* with a consonantal I, two syllables. *Ĭūlī* is three syllables, as at 1.556, 4.274 and 5.546. The fix is per gĕ-nĭ | tō(rem) ō | rō per | spēs sur | gen-tĭs Ĭ | ū-lī.
   - **6.375**: *iniussus* was read as four syllables, i-ni-us-sus. The i after the prefix is consonantal, as in *iniuria* (1.27). The fix is Eu-mĕ-nĭ | (dum) as-pĭ-cĭ | ēs rī | (pam-ve) in | ius-sŭs ă | dī-bis.
9. **Note 313–314**: "The second line has been admired … for what its slow spondees … say". Line 314 is not spondaic: tēn-dē | bānt-quĕ mă | nūs rī | (pae) ul-tĕ-rĭ | ō-rĭs ă | mō-re has three dactyls. The four slow spondees are in 313 (Stābānt | ōrān | tēs prī | mī trāns). Corrected.
10. **383, `gaudet cognomine terrae`**: `i` "he takes joy in a land that will bear his name" rendered the Latin Library's *terra* (a land of the same name), not Greenough's *terrae*. `i` is now "he is glad that a land will be called by his name". `l` is now "he rejoices in the surname of the land", matching the note's "the land's surname". The note itself is correct on both readings and is kept.
11. **Note 296–297**: "'Caeno vastaque voragine' are ablatives of description". `Caeno` goes with `turbidus` ("thick with mud") and is an ablative of cause. Only `vasta voragine` is manner or description. Fixed.

### Low
12. Note 295: "'Quae' stands second … 'Tartarei… Acherontis' frames the relative clause" was muddled, since both words belong inside the relative clause. It now says that `Tartarei` is put before `quae` for weight and that it and `Acherontis` wrap round `quae fert`.
13. l 300: "white hair" is now "grey hair", to match the note's "greyness".
14. i 298–300: "terrible in his squalor" echoed a well-known version. It is now "a fearsome figure in his filth; a mass of grey beard lies uncombed upon his chin".
15. i 300–301: "a filthy cloak hangs from his shoulders by a knot" echoed. It is now "a grimy cloak, knotted at the shoulder, hangs down from him".
16. Note 302: "'velis' a dative" was stated flatly. The note now also gives the instrumental-ablative reading ("works the boat with sails").
17. i 304: "a god's old age is hardy and green" echoed a well-known version. It is now "his is a god's old age, sturdy and still green".
18. i 305–308: "came streaming … young men laid on the pyre before their parents' eyes" was a distinctive echo. It is now "was pouring and surging down to the banks … boys and girls who never married, and youths set on the pyre while their parents looked on".
19. l 305: "Here" for `Huc` is now "Hither".
20. i 309–312 (the leaves and birds simile): "as many as the leaves … flock to land from the deep sea … sends them to sunny countries" ran close to known versions. It is now "many as the leaves that drift loose and drop in the forests when autumn's first cold comes, many as the birds that mass and make for land out of the deep … launching them towards sun-warmed lands".
21. i 313–314: "in longing for the farther shore" is the best-known phrase of the passage. It is now "their hands held out in desire for the bank beyond". `l` gives the literal "with love of the farther bank", as the note glosses it.
22. Note 317: the `enim` explanation was muddled ("not quite 'for' at the start of a clause"). The note keeps the parenthetical-causal reading ("Aeneas (for he was amazed…) says"), which is right, and adds the old asseverative alternative ("indeed").
23. Note 321: "'Olli' is Greenough's old form". It is Virgil's archaism, not an editor's spelling, and now reads "the archaic form of 'illi'".
24. i 322–324: "by whose power the gods dread to swear" echoed a well-known version. It is now "the water whose majesty the gods themselves are afraid to swear by and then betray".
25. Note 322–324 was trimmed: the sentence on Cocytus and Styx as one water repeated note 296–297. Without the trim, item 5 would have pushed the note past the validator's 140-word warning.
26. i 325–326 (flagged): "those the water carries are the buried" echoed. It is now "The whole crowd before you is the poor, unburied dead; the ferryman there is Charon; those borne on the water have been laid in their graves".
27. Note 325–326: "Three clauses, three answers to Aeneas's three questions" was not true, since nobody asked who the ferryman was. It now reads "Three short clauses answer him point by point, two of them without a verb".
28. i 331–332: "pitying in his heart their unjust lot" was close to a known version. It is now "his heart full of pity for their cruel lot".
29. Note 333–336: "'Leucaspim' and 'Oronten' are Greek accusatives". Only `Oronten` is Greek; `Leucaspim` is the Latin -im accusative. Fixed.
30. l 334: "of Lycia's the leader fleet" is now "the leader of Lycia's fleet", because coherence wins ties.
31. i 341–342: "Which of the gods, Palinurus, took you from us and drowned you" echoed. It is now "Palinurus, what god was it that stole you from us and sank you deep in mid-ocean?"
32. i 343: "Tell me, come." was not real English and is now "Come, tell me." `l` keeps the literal order.
33. i 343–346: "whom I never before found false … reach the shores of Ausonia" echoed a known version. It is now "who had never once proved false to me before, cheated my hopes with this single answer: he sang that you would … arrive within the bounds of Ausonia". "Bounds" is closer to `fines`.
34. Note 349–351: "Book V (858) also has the helm torn away". The helm is at 5.859 and the torn-off piece of stern at 858. The line number was dropped and the sentence made exact: thrown in with the helm and a piece of the stern torn away.
35. i 355–357: "at the fourth dawn, lifted high on the crest of a wave" echoed. It is now "only with the fourth day, as a wave lifted me up on its summit, did I catch sight of Italy". `vix` is taken as "only".
36. Note 355–357: added that in Book V the sea was calm the night he fell (5.848), so the storm here is another seam, as the note on 347–348 says of Somnus.
37. i 358–361: "clutched with crooked fingers … in their ignorance taken me for a prize" echoed. Rewritten: "had not a savage people, not knowing who I was and thinking me worth the plundering, set on me with steel as I hung there, dragged down by my sodden clothes, clawing with bent fingers at the rough crags of a headland".
38. i 362 (flagged): "Now the waves have me" echoed a well-known version. It is now "Now I belong to the sea, and the winds keep turning me over at the water's edge".
39. i 363–366 (flagged 365): "by the sweet light of heaven and the air … unconquered one … — you can —" echoed two known versions. Rewritten: "So by the dear daylight of the sky and the breath of air, … I entreat you, hero whom nothing has defeated, deliver me from these torments: either scatter earth on me, for that is in your power, and make for the harbour at Velia".
40. i 367–371 (flagged 371): "give your hand to a man in misery … so that at least in death I may find a quiet resting-place" ran word for word with a known version. It is now "reach your right hand to a wretched man … so that death at least may give me a quiet home to rest in".
41. i 374–375 was lightly rephrased away from a known version: "Will you, still unburied, set eyes on … or come to its bank without leave?"
42. i 376 (flagged): "Give up hoping that pleading will turn the gods' decrees" followed the shape of a well-known version. It is now "Hope no more that the gods' decrees will yield to entreaty."
43. i 377: "take what I say to heart, as a comfort in your hard fortune" echoed. It is now "hear what I tell you and remember it, a consolation in your cruel fortune".
44. i 378–381: "the place will bear the name of Palinurus for ever" echoed. It is now "for all time the spot will be called by Palinurus's name".
45. l 382–383: "from his heart was the grief, sad heart" was garbled. It is now "from his heart was the grief, from his sad heart".
46. Note 392–394: "grandson of Alceus" is now "Alcaeus". "'Thesea' and 'Pirithoum' are Greek accusatives" was half wrong: `Pirithoum` is the ordinary Latin accusative. Fixed.
47. Note 395–396: "the last of Hercules' labours, told by his own shade in Odyssey 11 (623–626)". Homer's Heracles calls it the hardest, not the last, so the note now says "the hardest", "as his own shade tells Odysseus". i: "The one came …" is now "The first of them came with his own hands to put Tartarus's watchdog in chains, and dragged him away cowering from beside the king's own throne".
48. Note 397: "Theseus will be seen later in this book" was not accurate, because he is not seen: the Sibyl names him in Tartarus. It now reads "Theseus is named later in this book, sitting there for ever (617–618)".

## Hand-scan notes on the special lines (scanner right, no entry)
- **Proper names**:
  - Ăchĕrōntis (295) and Cōcȳtō (297) are correct; *Cocyto eructat* elides.
  - Chărōn (299, 326) is correct.
  - Lēucāspim (334, eu one syllable, -im elided before *et*) is correct.
  - Ŏrōnten (334) is correct.
  - Anchīsiădē (348) is correct.
  - Pălĭnūrĕ (341, 373) and Pălĭnūrī (381) are correct.
  - Vĕlīnōs (366) is correct.
  - Eumenidum (375): Eu- is right; the line's only error is *iniussus*.
  - Alcīdēn (392, *vero* elided) is correct.
  - Thēsĕă Pīrĭthŏumque (393) is correct.
  - Ausonios (346) and Notus (355) are correct.
- **Initial Ae-**: Aeneas occurs only at 317 (fixed). aequora, aequore, aestuat and aeternum are correct.
- **Consonantal i after a prefix**: iniussus 375 is fixed. inice 366 is discussed below. ĭnīquam (332, *in + aequus*, a true vowel) is correct.
- **Hiatus**: there is none in this stretch. *Dic ait O virgo* (318) has *ait* as two short syllables and *O* before a consonant. *o Palinure* (373) is correct.
- **Elision and prodelision**: *fata est* (321), *turba est* (325), *via est* (367), *Umbrarum hic* (390), *iam inde* (385), *iam istinc* (389), *eripe me his* (365) and *Tartareum ille* (395) are all correct.

## Doubtful quantities left as scanned
- **6.366 *inice***: the scanner divides it i–ni⏑ce⏑. The true division is in-jĭ-cĕ (first syllable long by position, the vowel i short). The marks are identical (–⏑⏑), so no entry was added. The audio may lengthen the first i (see Questions). The same holds for aeneid-042's *coniciunt*.
- **6.299 and 6.350 *cui***: taken as one long syllable. A disyllabic *cu-i* would also fit 299 (Cha-ron cu-i dactyl). The monosyllable is Virgil's norm.
- **6.312 *ăprīcis***: the scanner's short a is the only fit in this line (mīt-tĭ-tă | prī-cīs).
- **6.396 *ipsĭus***: short i, the only fit.
- **6.385 *iam inde***: the scanner elides the whole of *iam*, which gives the same count as j(am) inde.

## Refused findings
- **R1 — 6.318 "Dic ait O virgo"** with no marks round `ait`. Confirmed as Greenough's habit: the source prints “Vade ait O felix…”, “testor numen ait…”, “sed moriamur ait…” and “Egredere o quicumque es ait…” the same way. It is not a misprint. `t` is as printed; `l` and `i` punctuate naturally; the note's wording is accurate. Kept.
- **R2 — 317 `enim`**: the parenthetical "for he was amazed" is the reading of the school commentaries and is right. It is kept, softened only by adding the alternative (item 22).
- **R3 — 327–328 `transportare` with `datur`**: the impersonal `datur` with the infinitive as subject, and the trans-compound taking an accusative of the thing crossed with the persons left unstated, are both correct. Kept.
- **R4 — 351–354 `tantum… quam` with `me` understood**: correct. `tantum… quam` is "so great… as", completed by the fear clause, and the subject accusative is omitted after `iuro` because it is the speaker. Kept.
- **R5 — 383 note on `cognomine terrae` and the variant `terra`**: both constructions offered for *terra* (the land as subject, or *cognomine* as the ablative of the adjective *cognominis*) are standard. Kept; only `l` and `i` were changed (item 10).
- **R6 — memory claims checked and kept**:
  - *Libyco cursu* (338) as a loose thread, since in Book V he falls between Sicily and Italy.
  - *nec me deus aequore mersit* (348) against Somnus in 5.838–861.
  - "No such oracle is reported earlier in the poem": Neptune's promise at 5.814–815 that one man will be lost is not an oracle of safety.
  - The Velia anachronism (366) "as ancient readers already noted": Hyginus, quoted by Gellius, faulted it.
  - The Lucanian plague and oracle at 379, from Servius.
  - Homer: Od. 10.513 (Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus into Acheron), Od. 11.36–41, 11.51–80, 11.57–58, 11.66–78 and 11.623–626, Il. 15.37–38, 23.71–74, 6.146 and 3.3–5.
  - Hesiod, *Theogony* 775–806 (Styx, and the forsworn god breathless for a year).
  - Georgics 4.475–477 = Aen. 6.306–308.
  - 6.197 *vestigia pressit*.
  - Aen. 1.113–117 for Orontes.
  - 6.260 and 6.290 for the drawn sword.
  - *portitor* as a harbour-dues collector (L&S).
  - Aristophanes' *Frogs* for Charon.
  - Pirithous as a son of Zeus (Il. 14) and Theseus as a son of Neptune.
  - Cape Palinuro.
- **R7 — note lengths**: units 337 (166 words), 363 (153) and 367 (146) exceed the validator's 140-word warning. They are the drafter's notes and each sentence earns its place. This is a warning, not a failure, so they are kept.
- **R8 — i 318 "said"** for the historic present `ait`. The English narrative past is fine. Kept.
- **R9 — i 390–391, 392–394, 385–387**: these are close to the literal sense, with no distinctive borrowed phrasing. Kept.
- **R10 — note 297 "the stream Charon crosses is called by turns Acheron, Cocytus (323) and the Styx (385)"**: accurate. Kept.
- **R11 — note 372, "the inverted 'cum' again"**: the label is right (main clause in the pluperfect, `cum` with the indicative giving the event). Kept.
- **R12 — note 358–361**, the indicative `tenebam` in a contrary-to-fact apodosis: correct (A&G on the imperfect indicative of action begun). Kept.

## For the owner (QUESTIONS.md)
- The scanner's syllable division for prefix + consonantal i, where the count is unchanged (*inice* i–ni–ce, *coniciunt* in 042), puts a long mark on a vowel that is short. If the audio reads long vowels from `sc`, these words may be mispronounced. Should such lines get hand entries anyway? The reviewers of 042 and 043 left them as scanned.
